content:
8 min read 1 hour ago -- Gjallarhorn is a Rails-class framework built from primitives in Odin — a hand-rolled HTTP server, a PostgreSQL wire client, an ORM, and a template engine, with zero dependencies. Here’s why that constraint is the whole point. Odin’s standard library has no HTTP server. No net/http, no client, no TLS. If you want to answer a request, you get a TCP socket and a byte slice, and the rest is yours. Most people treat that as a reason not to build web software in Odin. I treated it as a specification. Gjallarhorn is what came out: a small, honest web framework where the server, the router, the middleware, the templating, and the data access are all hand-built — and where the PostgreSQL driver talks the v3 wire protocol directly, because there’s no libpq to lean on either. The default build has no third-party packages. Just core:, base:, and about 6,700 lines of code you can read top to bottom in an afternoon. That last sentence is the thesis. Everything else in this post is a consequence of it. Repo: github.com/Lvcky-gg/Gjallarhorn · Arch users: yay -S gjallarhorn-git Why build from primitives The honest answer is that I wanted to understand the thing I run in production. Not “understand” in the sense of having read the docs — understand in the sense of being able to open any file and explain why every byte on the wire is where it is. When you npm install a framework, you inherit a supply chain: the framework, its dependencies, their dependencies, and the transitive trust that all of them are correct and none of them are hostile. For a lot of software that trade is fine. For a web framework — the thing that sits on the trust boundary, parsing attacker-controlled bytes all day — I wanted the surface to be small enough that "read it before you trust it" is an instruction a person can actually follow. So the design rule is severe and load-bearing: a new dependency is a design decision, not a convenience. The default build has none, and that’s a feature people rely on. It means the reason to trust Gjallarhorn isn’t my reputation or a green CI badge. It’s that you can read every line that touches your request. This is not a claim that hand-rolled code is safer than a mature library. It obviously isn’t, in the general case — libpq has had more eyes on it than I will ever have. The claim is narrower: for this project, with these goals, a readable whole beats an opaque sum. Sovereignty over the stack is worth the cost of building the stack. The framework speaks Norse, on purpose Gjallarhorn is the horn Heimdall sounds at the gates of Ásgarð — the alarm at the boundary. The naming isn’t decoration; it’s a thinking tool. Each name commits me to a metaphor, and the metaphor keeps the abstraction honest. • The request/response object is the Bifrost — the bridge each request crosses. Never “context.” A context is a bag of whatever; a bridge has two ends and a thing guarding it. • Middleware are runes — inscriptions layered around the handler, an onion you pass through inward and unwind outward. • Auth guards are wards — a ward admits or refuses; that’s its whole job. • The template engine is Loom, and rendering is weaving: your data (the weft) run through a template (the warp). • The ORM is Mímir, after the well of memory. Its database handle is a well; you recall rows from it and offer rows to it. • Static files are served by hail — you hail a directory into the app. When the vocabulary is coherent, the API almost writes itself, and so does the mental model. You don’t memorize verbs; you ask what the metaphor would do. A minimal app Here’s a whole application. Note the shape before the details: everything is a free procedure taking the app or the Bifrost by pointer. Odin has no methods and no UFCS, so it’s gh.get(&app, ...), never app.Get(...). That's not a limitation I worked around — it's a clarity I kept. package mainimport gh "gjallarhorn"User :: struct { id: int `db:"id,pk,auto"`, name: string `db:"name,notnull"`, }hello :: proc(b: ^gh.Bifrost) { name, _ := gh.param(b, "name") gh.json(b, 200, User{id = 1, name = name}) }main :: proc() { app := gh.new(gh.Config{ port = 8091, secret = "set-me-in-production", db_type = .Postgres, postgres = gh.Postgres_Config{ host = "127.0.0.1", port = 5432, user = "app", password = "secret", dbname = "gjallarhorn", }, }) // Middleware ("runes"), registered onion-style, outermost first. gh.rune(&app, gh.logger) gh.rune(&app, gh.cors) // Let Mímir remember the model; its table is auto-migrated at run(). gh.remember(&app, User) gh.get(&app, "/hello/:name", hello) gh.hail(&app, "/static", "./public") gh.run(&app) }Run it with odin run .. No database? Leave dbname empty — migrations print the DDL they would run, the DB routes return 503, and everything else works. The framework tells you the truth about its own state rather than pretending. Walking the onion A request crosses the Bifrost through a stack of runes, hits a ward, reaches your handler, and unwinds back out. Each layer has exactly one job and one security checkpoint. Runes: middleware without closures Odin has no closures. In most languages middleware captures “the rest of the chain” in a closure; I can’t. So the remaining chain is threaded through explicitly — you call next(b) to descend, or you don't, to stop. auth :: proc(b: ^gh.Bifrost, next: gh.Next) { if !authorized(b) { gh.text(b, 401, "nope") return // don't call next → chain stops here } next(b) // descend into the next layer }gh.rune(&app, auth)The absence of closures forced the control flow into the open, where you can see it. That’s the recurring theme with Odin: the constraint you’d expect to fight turns into the feature you’d have wanted anyway. Built-in runes: logger (one structured line per request, colorized on a TTY, plain when piped), cors, csrf, rate_limit, plus request_id and metrics (a real Prometheus exposition at /metrics). Wards: a guard is just a predicate A ward is proc(b: ^Bifrost) -> bool. Return true to admit; on false the handler is skipped and dispatch falls back to 401. It's an optional 4th argument to any route. gh.get(&app, "/account", account_handler, gh.require_login)That’s the entire auth-guard mechanism. Roles, ownership checks, feature flags — they’re all just predicates you write. There’s no policy DSL to learn because a boolean function already is one. Mímir: the ORM, where SQL injection is the checkpoint Your struct is the schema; db: tags drive migration, binding, and hydration. The query verbs follow the well's vocabulary — recall (SELECT), offer (INSERT), amend (UPDATE), forget (DELETE), carve (CREATE TABLE). w := gh.well(b)q := gh.recall(w, User) gh.whose(&q, "id = ?", 7) // value is BOUND, never interpolated gh.limit(&q, 1)rows, ok := gh.query(w, gh.sql(&q)) user, found := gh.scan_one(rows, User) // (User, bool)The checkpoint here is stated plainly and enforced structurally: values never reach the SQL string. Every value is a bound parameter ($1.. on Postgres, ? elsewhere). You can write a raw fragment for the WHERE clause, but the values in it are always parameters. The API makes the safe path the default path. Nullability is handled with Odin’s Maybe(T) rather than sentinel values, so NULL is never conflated with zero or empty — a distinction that has bitten every ORM that treated an empty string as the absence of a string: Event :: struct { id: int `db:"id,pk,auto"`, note: Maybe(string) `db:"note"`, // NULL → None, value → Some(v) }Loom: templates, autoescaped by default Loom is a Jinja subset pared to its load-bearing parts — {{ expr }} with filter pipelines, {% if %}/{% for %}, inheritance, includes, and macros. Output is HTML-autoescaped by default; you opt out with an explicit | safe, never in.

{{ title }}

Hail, {{ user.name }}{% if user.admin %} (admin){% endif %}.

{% if items %}
    {% for item in items %}
  1. #{{ loop.index }} — {{ item | upper }}{% if loop.last %} (last){% endif %}
    2. {% endfor %}
{% else %}

Nothing woven yet.

{% endif %}Escape-by-default is the same philosophy as bound parameters, applied to a different boundary: the dangerous operation should require you to ask for it, in writing, where a reviewer can see the ask. The part I’m proudest of is the part that broke A framework you can read is only worth something if you actually read it — adversarially, on a schedule, and then write down what you found. Gjallarhorn has been through several full-repo security audits, and the findings live in a public remediation backlog. Two of them are worth telling, because they’re exactly the bugs that “just use a library” is supposed to save you from — and exactly the bugs you only catch when you own the whole stack. The crash that was invisible in the logs. After a routine feature session, an AddressSanitizer sweep turned up a use-after-free that killed the server after a single templated render. Loom caches parsed template trees on the heap for reuse — but the cached nodes held include/extends names that pointed into a per-request temporary arena. The arena was reclaimed at the end of the request; the next render followed a dangling pointer into freed memory. It was in committed code, it produced no error in the logs, and it had nothing to do with what I'd been working on. The fix was one line — but the decision was the interesting part: fix it at the point of retention, not allocation. Making the lexer honor a longer-lived allocator would have leaked every render-time literal; cloning the string into the node allocator at the single point where the cache keeps it fixed the lifetime exactly where the lifetime was wrong. Owning the memory model meant I could reason about it. A garbage collector would have hidden the bug; a library would have hidden the code. The smuggling bug hiding in a stdlib call. The HTTP server parsed Content-Length with strconv.parse_int. Reasonable, until you notice that parse_int is not an RFC 1*DIGIT parser — it happily accepts 0x10, 1_0, +5, 0b1000. So a front-end proxy and Gjallarhorn could disagree about how long the body was, which is the raw material of an HTTP request-smuggling attack. The fix was strict is_decimal/is_hex validation before parsing, on both Content-Length and chunk sizes, rejecting anything non-canonical with a 400. The lesson isn’t “stdlib bad.” It’s that building from primitives means the primitives are your responsibility — including their sharp edges. That’s the cost side of the sovereignty trade, stated honestly. The framework’s own contributing standards put it bluntly: uncompiled code is untested, an unverified benchmark is not a result, and fabricating a security property is the one failure that erodes trust faster than any bug. Gjallarhorn documents what’s solid and what’s still open, because a framework that hides its weak points is asking for a trust it hasn’t earned. What the constraints taught me If I had to compress the whole project into one idea, it’s this: the constraints of the language and the discipline of no-dependencies both push in the same direction — toward code that has nowhere to hide. No closures, so control flow is explicit. No methods, so data flow is explicit. Errors are values, so failure is explicit. Manual memory, so lifetimes are explicit. No dependencies, so the trust surface is explicit. Every one of those is a place where a more “convenient” language would let me paper over a decision I hadn’t actually made. Odin makes me make it, and then makes me write it down. That’s not the right trade for every project or every team. But if what you want is to run something in production that you genuinely understand — every rune, every bound parameter, every byte of the wire protocol — then building from primitives isn’t the hard way. It’s the only way that gets you there. The horn is at the gate. You can read exactly how it’s built. Try it • Framework: github.com/Lvcky-gg/Gjallarhorn • Install on Arch: gjallarhorn-git on
